query: FeNiCrCoCu is considered suitable for thin-film use, and its expense favors applying it as a protective coating on conventional metals rather than using it in bulk. Earlier studies examined room-temperature wear behavior in relation to coating–substrate combinations, composition, and grain size, but largely addressed the alloy itself or a limited thermal regime rather than the overall wear response of a coating across different temperatures. Under the constraints that FeNiCrCoCu remains a thin protective coating and that high-temperature wear is the target application, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its overall wear resistance and why? Specify an intervention relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the observations expected if the hypothesis is correct, state the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, connect the hypothesis to prior evidence, and identify a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: For FeNiCrCoCu thin protective coatings used in high-temperature applications, a pre-formed, optimally thin and adherent Cr2O3 oxide layer mediates wear resistance by providing both a thermal barrier and a lubricating effect. In contrast, coatings lacking such a controlled oxide layer or developing excessively thick oxide scales will suffer from spallation and increased wear.
generation.material_initial_state: FeNiCrCoCu thin-film protective coating (e.g., microwave-cladded on SS-304) in the as-deposited state
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled pre-oxidation step (e.g., exposure to air at ~800 °C for a short duration) to promote the formation of a thin, continuous Cr2O3 layer, then subject the coating to high-temperature sliding wear tests under variable loads.
generation.conditions: High-temperature sliding wear tests performed in air over a temperature range of 600–900 °C and applied loads between 10 and 30 N, mimicking conditions for high-temperature protective coatings.
generation.structural_mediator: The stability, continuity, and thickness of the thermally induced Cr2O3 oxide layer at the coating surface.
generation.mechanism: The pre-formed Cr2O3 oxide layer, when maintained at an optimal thinness, acts as a barrier against further oxidation and thermal softening and reduces direct metal–counterbody contact. This lubricating layer lowers friction and wear. However, if the oxide layer becomes too thick or unstable, mechanical cycling leads to spallation and the formation of abrasive debris, which in turn increases wear rates.
generation.predicted_outcome: Coatings that receive the controlled pre-oxidation treatment will exhibit lower wear rates and reduced coefficients of friction during high-temperature sliding, relative to as-deposited coatings. A measurable optimum in oxide thickness (tentatively in the tens of nanometers range) should be observed, with performance degrading if the oxide scale is either absent or excessively thick and prone to spallation.
generation.baseline: As-deposited FeNiCrCoCu coating without pre-oxidation, tested under identical high-temperature wear conditions.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is confined to thin-film geometries under atmospheric air in the temperature range of 600–900 °C and sliding loads from 10 to 30 N; results may not directly extend to bulk materials or other environmental conditions.
generation.uncertainty: While evidence (PMC10908794::web::037::microstructure_investigation and PMC10908794::web::051::wear_behavior) supports the formation of protective oxide layers that enhance wear resistance, there is uncertainty regarding the optimal oxide thickness and its stability in thin-film form, as well as the transition point at which the oxide layer becomes deleterious by spallation. This study extends findings from bulk or simulation regimes to the thin-film, high-temperature wear scenario.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu thin coatings on identical substrates. One set receives a controlled pre-oxidation treatment designed to form a thin Cr2O3 layer, while the other remains as-deposited. Subject both sets to sliding wear tests at 600, 750, and 900 °C under loads of 10, 20, and 30 N. Characterize the oxide layer thickness and integrity pre- and post-test using SEM, EDS, and XRD.
measurements: Coefficient of friction during sliding tests
Oxide layer thickness and morphology pre- and post-wear via SEM/EDS
Adhesion and spallation events observed by high-resolution imaging
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-oxidized coatings do not consistently show lower wear rates and a reduced coefficient of friction compared to as-deposited coatings across the tested temperatures and loads, or if no clear correlation between a specific oxide layer thickness and improved wear resistance is observed, the hypothesis that a controlled thin Cr2O3 layer is the primary mediator of enhanced high-temperature wear resistance will be falsified.
